description: A field guide to insects, spiders, and other creepy-crawlies written for 8–12 year olds by Wikijunior volunteers. Each page tells what a bug looks like, where it lives, what it eats, and how it defends itself. Each day you read one or two pages together, sketch the bug in a journal, and head outside to look for it. It's a free, openly licensed book; every page is free to read on Wikibooks.
includes: Link to the free Wikibooks page for every lesson
A bug journal page for every creature
Short outdoor bug hunts and simple at-home observations
Questions with answers for every lesson

lessons.title: Lesson 1: Crazy Bug Facts and Insects
steps: Read both pages together
Start a bug journal and draw an insect's three body parts
Narrate how scientists sort living things into groups
questions: What are the smallest insects in the world?
How many legs does an insect have?

steps: Read the page together
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen

questions: Who lays the eggs in an ant colony?

lessons.title: Lesson 9: Crickets
steps: Read the page together
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen
Listen for crickets on a warm evening
questions: How do crickets make their sound?

answers: By rubbing a scraper on a toothed vein on the wing
Crickets have longer antennae and are usually brown or black

questions: How does a walking stick hide?
Why is a praying mantis called that?
answers: It looks like a twig and sways like a branch
Its front legs look like it is praying

lessons.title: Lesson 13: Shield Bugs and Stink Bugs

Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen

answers: They give off a bad smell when disturbed

About how many kinds of ladybugs live in the world?

lessons.title: Lesson 15: Fireflies
steps: Read the page together
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen

units.title: Unit 3: Flies, Biters and Water Bugs

lessons.title: Lesson 16: House Flies and Fruit Flies
steps: Read both pages
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen

questions: What can house flies taste with?

answers: By the markings on their wings

lessons.title: Lesson 17: Mosquitoes, Black Flies and Crane Flies
steps: Read the three pages
Make a chart: which of these bite, and why?
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen
questions: Why does a female mosquito drink blood?
Does a crane fly bite like a mosquito?
answers: To get nutrients for her eggs
No; it only looks like a giant mosquito

lessons.title: Lesson 18: Fleas and Lice
steps: Read both pages
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen
Talk about how pets are kept free of fleas
questions: Do fleas have wings?
Can head lice jump or fly?

lessons.title: Lesson 19: Dragonflies and Damselflies
steps: Read the dragonfly and damselfly pages (the third page is extra reading)
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen
Visit a pond and watch them hunt
questions: How can you tell a damselfly from a dragonfly at rest?
What do dragonflies eat?
answers: A damselfly folds its wings over its body; a dragonfly holds them out flat
Other insects, such as flies and mosquitoes

lessons.title: Lesson 20: Mayflies
steps: Read the page together
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen
Look for mayfly nymphs under stones in a stream
questions: Why are mayflies sometimes called dayflies?
How many long 'tails' trail behind a mayfly?
answers: They live for a very short time as adults

lessons.title: Lesson 21: Water Beetles and Water Striders
steps: Read the three pages
Float a paper clip on water to see surface tension
Sketch it in your bug journal and label head, thorax and abdomen
questions: How do diving beetles swim?
Why don't water striders sink?
answers: They paddle with flat, hairy back legs
Water-repelling hairs keep their legs dry on the surface

steps: Read both pages
Sketch it in your bug journal and count its legs
Find a web and see if you can spot the spider
questions: How many legs does a spider have?
Where does a spider's silk come from?
Is a spider an insect?

lessons.title: Lesson 23: Spiders That Hunt
steps: Read the three pages
Sketch it in your bug journal and count its legs
Look in flowers for a crab spider
questions: Where do wolf spider babies ride?
How does a crab spider move?
answers: Sideways and backward, like a crab

lessons.title: Lesson 24: Spiders That Build
steps: Read the three pages
Draw an orb web, a funnel web and a trapdoor burrow
Spray a web lightly with water to see its pattern
questions: What do trapdoor spiders use the spines on their jaws for?
How many eyes do orb weavers have?

lessons.title: Lesson 25: Spiders to Watch Out For
steps: Read the three pages
Learn what a black widow and a brown recluse look like, and never touch one
Sketch it in your bug journal and count its legs
questions: What mark does a black widow have?
How many eyes does a brown recluse have?

lessons.title: Lesson 26: Tarantulas

Sketch it in your bug journal and count its legs
Narrate how tree-living tarantulas climb smooth leaves
questions: What are the largest spiders in the world?
Where does the Mexican red-knee get its name?
answers: Red or orange hair on its leg joints

lessons.title: Lesson 27: Scorpions and Pseudoscorpions
steps: Read the three pages
Sketch it in your bug journal and count its legs
Compare a scorpion and a pseudoscorpion
questions: What happens when ultraviolet light shines on a scorpion?
Does a pseudoscorpion have a stinger?

steps: Read the three pages
Sketch it in your bug journal and count its legs

Why should we check ourselves for ticks?

steps: Read both pages
Dig gently in garden soil and look for worms
Narrate why worms are good for soil
questions: How does an earthworm get oxygen?
Where do earthworms live?

lessons.title: Lesson 30: Centipedes and Millipedes
steps: Read both pages
Draw both and compare: legs per segment
Go on a short bug hunt and look for one
questions: How many pairs of legs does a millipede have on each segment?
Does a millipede really have a thousand legs?

lessons.title: Lesson 31: Woodlice (Pill Bugs)
steps: Read the page together
Look under a damp log or flowerpot for roly-polies
Sketch it in your bug journal and count its body segments

links.label: Read: Woodlouse, Pill Bug or Armadillo Bug

questions: What group of animals are woodlice part of, like crabs and shrimp?
What do some woodlice do to protect themselves?

lessons.title: Lesson 32: Glossary and Review
steps: Read through the glossary and pick five new words
Make a chart: insects, arachnids, and other bugs
Choose your favorite bug and tell why
questions: How many body parts does an insect have?
Name one arachnid that is not a spider.
answers: Any one: scorpion, tick, mite, harvestman
